title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Dust Heap and the Drawing Room

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do to get it.
It is also, perhaps, the strangest and most labyrinthine thing Dickens ever built.
A fortune founded on dust heaps — literal mounds of Victorian London's waste — rises, changes hands, corrupts, and occasionally redeems.
To read it with me today, I am joined by three guests whose combined knowledge of this novel is, frankly, intimidating.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the most distinguished literary critics of his generation.
He reads novels as moral investigations — as stories about character, conscience, and the trials that reveal what people are truly made of.
Oliver Trevelyan needs little introduction to anyone who has ever listened to a classic novel on a long drive.
He has voiced more great audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive, and he comes to Dickens as a performer — hearing every comic rhythm, every grotesque, every pause written for the voice.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and a passionate, lifelong reader of Victorian fiction.
She came to this novel as a teenager, has read it many times since, and cares deeply about what it feels like to read — what stops you, what moves you, what makes you go back and re-read a sentence.
Today we begin at the top — with the dust heap fortune, the mansion it buys, and the shadow of greed that falls over everything from the very first pages.
The very first thing to say about this novel is that its premise is, on the face of it, completely absurd.
A man inherits a vast fortune because his father spent his life accumulating the rubbish of London.
And Dickens — with absolute seriousness and absolute comic genius simultaneously — takes that premise and runs with it for nine hundred pages.
Now, our hero of the dust — Nicodemus Boffin — has installed himself in this grand mansion, and Dickens can't resist.
He tells us that, like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites.
An aristocratic family cheese.
I have read that line aloud professionally and I still cannot get through it without wanting to pause and simply admire it.
The comic precision of it — the way it lands — is pure Dickens at the top of his game.
One must acknowledge that the cheese is extraordinarily good.
But I would resist the temptation to treat it merely as a comic flourish and move on.
What is remarkable about the passage — and about Boffin from the beginning — is his contentment.
He regards the parasites, the excess, the sheer incongruity of his situation — as, Dickens tells us, a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty.
He pays it willingly, because Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was delighted.
That is not the portrait of a man corrupted by wealth.
That is the portrait of a good man — made temporarily ridiculous by fortune, but not diminished by it.
What strikes me re-reading this passage — and I've read it many times — is that single phrase: the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour.
Dickens immediately undercuts it — or in less cutting language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire — but the sting is real.
There is a whole social world in that cutting language — people who will call Boffin a worm simply because he came from nothing.
And that is the world into which he has arrived — the world of the aristocratic family cheese, with its infinite amount of parasites.
Dickens is funny, yes — but the comedy here carries a very quiet fury underneath it.
And then there is the other side of all this — what the dust heap fortune attracts beyond aristocratic parasites.
Enter Silas Wegg — one of the great villainous comic creations in all of English fiction.
Wegg has got hold of a document — a later will — that he believes gives him power over Boffin.
And so he cannot rest without hovering over Boffin's house — Dickens calls him the Evil Genius of it — simply savouring that power.
Power — unless it be the power of intellect or virtue — has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures.
The mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.
A house of cards.
Wegg can't do anything with his power yet — he just wants to stand outside and feel it.
That passage about power and low natures is one of the most direct moral pronouncements in the entire novel.
Dickens speaks in his own voice — the omniscient narrator steps forward and states a truth plainly.
And it is, I think, exactly right — not as social theory but as observation of human nature.
Wegg does not want money particularly — he wants to feel superior.
He wants to hover, and to know he could destroy.
There is something deeply, recognisably petty about that — and something rather frightening.
And what Wegg holds over Boffin connects back to that earlier will — the document that shapes the entire plot.
Wegg reads it out — performing it, really — and it has this wonderful bluntness to it.
Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him.
Quite enough for him.
That is old John Harmon speaking from beyond the grave — contemptuous, solitary, still punishing everyone around him.
The whole sad, bitter world of the Harmon fortune is compressed into that single little phrase.
So from the very foundations of this novel — the dust heaps, the mansion, the will, the parasites both parasitic and predatory — we already have the whole moral architecture of what's to come.
Money arrives, and it immediately sorts people — into the contented, the corrupted, and the merely hovering.
In our next segment, we'll follow that money further — into the drawing rooms and the river — and ask what this novel does with the people it destroys along the way.

segments.title: Bella's Refusal: Desire, Marriage, and Self-Knowledge

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
Today we're deep inside one of the novel's most intricate emotional territories: Bella Wilfer, John Rokesmith, and the question of what it actually means to choose a person over a fortune.
With me, as ever, are three readers whose company I find indispensable.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the moral philosopher's eye — the conviction that great fiction is finally about character tested, not ideology illustrated.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more of this novel aloud than almost anyone alive, and hears rhythms in the prose that the rest of us have to be shown.
And Caroline Woodcourt comes as a reader who fell in love with this book young and has never quite recovered — which is, I think, the right condition for discussing it.
Let's begin with John Harmon himself — or rather, with the man who cannot quite bring himself to be John Harmon.
What strikes me first about these chapters is how Dickens insists on Harmon's self-examination as a moral act in itself.
There is that extraordinary moment where Harmon interrogates himself aloud, checks the verdict, and confirms it.
He says, and I want to read this carefully:
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple repetition — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — is not rhetoric for an audience.
It is a man taking his own measure, in private, with genuine dread of what he might find.
And then the self-correction — 'Is that so? That is exactly so' — which is Johnson-like in its severity toward oneself.
Edmund, yes — but hear it as performance and it becomes something almost unbearable.
The whole passage is written for the voice, not the page.
When you read that aloud, the 'shrinking' doesn't build to a climax — it contracts, it shrinks, exactly as the word promises.
And then, in the next chapter, we get the same mind going over it all again — but now tracing the logic of how deception compounds itself.
Dickens sets it up with this devastating sentence:
'He had lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
'Accumulative power of its separate circumstances' — there is the whole tragedy of this novel in a subordinate clause.
What moves me in that same passage is the impossible bind Dickens constructs for Harmon.
He can come back to life and buy Bella — or come back and punish her by rejecting the inheritance.
Dickens puts it with a terrible bluntness: 'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
That question — shame or meanness — leaves no honourable door open.
And yet Bella herself is never consulted. She is the object of all this moral geometry.
Which is itself a kind of violence — however tenderly intended.
I take your point, Caroline, though I'd be cautious about pressing the modern frame too far onto the Victorian marriage plot.
What Dickens is dramatising is not Harmon's failure to consult Bella — it is his terror of his own inheritance and its power to corrupt.
The deception was, as the text tells us, conceived in distrust engendered by a wretched childhood — not in calculation or malice.
The father and his wealth acted, in Dickens's own phrase, 'for evil — never yet for good' on everyone within their influence.
That is the moral inheritance Harmon is trying to escape. Not merely a legal one.
And it's against that background — the corrupting pressure of money — that we have to read the Boffin scenes.
Because Boffin is meant to be Bella's mirror — showing her what she could become if she follows the money.
And that mirror is horrifying when Dickens finally shows it to us directly.
Bella steals a look at Boffin, and the prose does something extraordinarily spare.
Just this:
'A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
Six words at the end — 'the once open face' — do the work of a paragraph of backstory.
We remember who Boffin was. And that memory is what makes it a tragedy, not just a satire.
And then Dickens gives Boffin a speech that is almost unbearable in its comic awfulness.
He tells Bella, with great relish, exactly what she should do with her life.
'Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.'
'R—r—rich!' — with that extraordinary stammer Dickens writes in.
It's greed performing itself. Greed enjoying its own voice.
And Bella has to sit there and receive it.
That's the test. That's precisely the test.
It is indeed the test — and one must note that Dickens elsewhere in this same chapter turns the same satirical lance on philanthropic vanity.
Boffin's contempt for the charity patrons is, in its way, the obverse of his own avarice — a man who sees through pretension even as he succumbs to it.
The passage about the patronesses is worth quoting, because it shows Dickens calibrating the comedy with precision:
'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses' — and so it spirals.
The list is the joke. Burke would have called it the proliferation of empty dignities.
I've read that speech aloud to audiences and it always gets a laugh — but then the laugh catches in the throat.
Because it's not merely funny. It's Boffin auditing the world's hypocrisy from inside his own corruption.
And there's a quieter passage I keep returning to — Rokesmith, watching from a doorway.
Dickens writes:

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
That sentence holds three worlds at once — Betty Higden's courage, Bella's isolation, and Rokesmith's silent longing.
All in one long, unhurried, devastating sentence.
The 'boofer lady' is such an extraordinary touch.
It's Johnny's word for Bella — a dying child's word — and Rokesmith is still using it, privately, inside his own grief.
The narrator slips into his register without announcing it. You have to catch it.
And that, for me, is why Bella's arc works — because the love watching her is never announced.
It simply waits.
'It simply waits' — which is, I think, exactly what this segment of the novel does to the reader as well.
We've been circling Bella's transformation from without — through Harmon's fear, Boffin's corruption, Rokesmith's silent vigil.
In our next segment, we'll move to Bella's own voice — what she chooses, and what that choice costs her.

segments.title: John Harmon's Second Life: Identity and Narrative Deception

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, and puts it back together again.
I'm joined today, as ever, by three readers whose company I find indispensable.
Sir Edmund Leigh — Oxford don, moral critic, and a man who will not let us reduce a great novel to a pamphlet.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook narrator, and arguably the person alive who has spent the most hours inside Dickens's prose.
And Caroline Woodcourt — critic and close reader, who has been returning to this novel since her teenage years and finds something new each time.
Today we're looking at the John Harmon strand — the disguised heir at the centre of this novel's most elaborate deception.

We have passages that span the arc: from the Boffins' tender defence of the boy, through Mrs Boffin's extraordinary proposal to adopt an orphan in his name, to the furious unmasking of Silas Wegg in the novel's closing movements.
Edmund — let's begin with the Boffins, because I think they are the emotional foundation on which the whole Harmon mystery rests.
Yes — and it's worth pausing on that, because the Boffins are often discussed as comic figures, warm-hearted simpletons elevated by fortune.
But in this passage, Boffin reveals something altogether more serious — a sustained moral courage exercised over years, in the face of genuine brutality.
He speaks with that extraordinary vernacular dignity that Dickens gives his best working characters — the sentence constructions are rough, but the moral perception is precise.
Listen to the way he sets up the climactic moment — there is a kind of relish in the telling, but the horror underneath it is entirely real.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
That parenthesis about the black straw bonnet is pure Dickens — the comedy and the savagery held in the same breath.
And then: "Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — the single verb repeated, stripped bare — is one of the most quietly devastating things in the novel.
Edmund is entirely right about that repetition — and I'll confess, when I recorded this book, I spent a long time on those two words.
Because the genius of it is the pause that Dickens writes into the syntax.
"Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood" — that comma after Lightwood is a full stop in disguise.
Boffin gathers himself. He makes sure Lightwood has understood. And then he says it again.
That is a man performing his own memory — not telling a story, but reliving one.
What strikes me further is what this passage does for the Harmon plot.
We're learning, through Boffin's dialect and grief, what John Harmon was worth to these people — long before the inheritance, long before the plot mechanics.
That's what makes his secret return so charged — these people genuinely loved the boy.
And then Mrs Boffin does something extraordinary with that love — she tries to extend it forward, to someone who doesn't yet exist.
The passage in which she proposes adopting an orphan and naming him John is one of those moments that shouldn't work — and absolutely does.
She frames it herself as a whim — disarms any sentimentality before we can object.
But the feeling underneath it is anything but a whim.
She says — and I want to read this exactly as written —
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
The accumulation of that sentence — "find," "take," "adopt," "give," "provide" — it's an act of will, not sentimentality.
And the irony, of course, is devastating — because the real John is standing right there, in the house, watching all of this, anonymous.
That irony is structural, and it is moral in the deepest sense.
Harmon chose to remain hidden — partly from caution, partly, one suspects, from a desire to know whether he was genuinely valued, or merely the vessel of an inheritance.
What Mrs Boffin's proposal does is answer that question — decisively, tenderly, and without knowing it is answering anything at all.
Burke wrote that the bonds of society are formed by the small platoons — the immediate loyalties.
The Boffins are precisely that — the loyalty that precedes and transcends the legal and financial machinery of the plot.
Which makes the Dutch bottle business — when we finally get to it — all the more satisfying.
Because by the time Harmon is confronting Wegg, we carry all that accumulated tenderness with us — and the rage lands differently.
The passage where he explains the bottle's contents is quite remarkable for its compressed exposition — Dickens packs in the whole hidden history in a single speech.
But the voice is not expository — it is furious. Harmon is shaking the man while he explains the plot to him.
Consider what he says about Boffin and the will —
"That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father."
"That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister — then already dead of a broken heart — by name."
The phrase "self-tormenting father" — that is the whole of the old man's tragedy in three words.
And "dead of a broken heart, by name" — Dickens doesn't soften it. The sister is named as reviled even in death.
That phrase has stayed with me across every re-reading — "dead of a broken heart, by name."
It is so compressed. The legal formality of "by name" placed against the most intimate cause of death imaginable.
And then there's the passage where Harmon explains how they watched Wegg — how Sloppy shadowed him all that time.
He tells Wegg that they let him run on precisely because they wanted his disappointment to be total.
There's something almost cold about it — and yet Wegg is so comprehensively villainous that you find yourself admiring the architecture of the trap.
Harmon says —
"I kept you under good observation from my first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow."
"The delight of his life" — that's Sloppy, the gentle giant, happily trailing this wretched man through every scheme.
There is something quietly comic in the image — and something very Dickensian about justice wearing the face of a cheerful shadow.
I want to return to the identity question, because I think it's where the novel's real seriousness lies.
Harmon's disguise is not merely a plot device — it is a test of selfhood under conditions of radical erasure.
He watches the people who loved the boy he was — and discovers whether they loved the person, or merely the position.
And what he discovers — through Boffin's grief, through Mrs Boffin's adoption proposal, through the burial of that damning will — is that genuine benevolence exists in the world.
There is a line in the confrontation with Wegg that carries the whole moral weight of the novel's ending —
"I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out."
One notices that even in this extremity, Harmon frames his fury in the language of permission — "for leave."
He is a man who has learned — at great cost — that there are limits one does not cross, even in the service of justice.
"For leave" — I love that Edmund caught that.
When I came to record that line, I realised it had to be read with absolute fury restrained by a hairsbreadth.
Because if Harmon simply explodes, the sentence loses its shape — and Dickens wrote it with great precision.
The whole confrontation has a performer's sense of structure — the revelation of the Dutch bottle contents, the tracking of Wegg's movements, the gradual closing of every exit.
Harmon has waited for this moment — possibly longer than the reader has — and he is not going to rush it.
What strikes me, pulling these passages together, is how tightly the novel binds identity to witness — to being seen and known by someone who chooses to value you.
Harmon's second life only becomes legible — only becomes real — because the Boffins were there before him, holding his first life in trust.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the river — that persistent, murky presence that opens this novel and never quite leaves it.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Laughter and Survival: The Comic Voice of Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — which means, among other things, taking its comedy seriously.
Today's segment is about laughter — about how this novel uses comic genius not as decoration but as a survival strategy.
With me are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes the novel's greatness lies in moral imagination — in how individuals meet, or fail to meet, the trials life sets before them.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive, and who comes to every book as a performer first.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong Dickens reader who cares most about the experience on the page — what makes you stop, re-read, catch your breath.
Oliver, I want to begin with you, because you have spent your professional life listening to how prose sounds — and this novel's comic voice is extraordinary.
It is extraordinary — and I think what makes it extraordinary is that the comedy is doing moral work at the same time as it's making you laugh.
Take the Lammles — this marvellously poisonous couple who have each tricked the other into a loveless marriage on false pretences of wealth.
The narrator watches them perform affection for their guests, perfectly, devastatingly.
And then comes this absolutely lethal aside — listen to this:
'How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out Here I am, suffocating in the closet!'
The skeleton in the closet — it's the oldest cliché in the language — and he makes it literal, and gives it a voice, and that voice is pathetic and desperate and somehow hilarious.
That is a writer at full stretch.
What gets me about that passage is the timing.
The narrator doesn't intrude while the scene is playing — he lets the performance run, lets you almost believe it —
and then drops the skeleton on you with that breezy 'for instance.'
That 'for instance' is doing so much work — it suggests the narrator has a whole list of moments he could have chosen, and this is merely one.
It's a very aristocratic form of cruelty, that 'for instance.'
I take the point about cruelty — though I would call it precision rather than cruelty.
What the comedy illuminates — what it always illuminates in this novel — is the exact mechanism of self-deception.
The Lammles are not merely fraudulent toward society — they are fraudulent toward themselves.
That is the moral substance beneath the wit.
Oliver, the Lammles reappear in a later scene — with young Fledgeby — that pushes this comic-moral engine still further.
Oh, this scene — this is Lammle at his most magnificently absurd.
He is threatening Fledgeby in the most pompous, chest-puffed, preposterous manner imaginable.
And the detail that kills me — 'making the most of his chest' — three words that demolish any dignity Lammle thinks he possesses.
Then he delivers this magnificent speech — I have to read it:

'This fellow presumes on my having in my desk round the corner, his dirty note of hand for a wretched sum payable on the occurrence of a certain event, which event can only be of my and my wife's bringing about!'
'This fellow, Fledgeby, presumes to be impertinent to me, Lammle. Give me your nose sir!'
Give me your nose, sir — I mean, it's spectacular.
The man is a complete fraud threatening another complete fraud, and the only weapon he can produce is a demand for someone's nose.
What I love about that speech is how the syntax performs the bluster.
'This fellow' — three times, that hammering repetition — it mimics a man working himself up, feeding his own outrage.
And underneath all the indignation, you can see the squalor of the actual arrangement — a dirty note of hand, a wretched sum.
The comedy doesn't let you forget what these people actually are.
The rhetorical inflation is perfectly judged.
Lammle speaks as a man of honour and is demonstrably nothing of the kind — and the distance between the register and the reality is where the comedy lives.
Burke wrote of men who mistake the language of virtue for its substance.
Lammle is a comic illustration of that perennial failure.
And Fledgeby gets his comeuppance — in a scene that I suspect Oliver has been wanting to reach since we began.
Miss Jenny Wren — Jenny Wren sprinkling pepper on Fledgeby's plasters — this is one of the great comic moments of the novel.
What's brilliant is the form of the enquiry she puts to herself.
She's not announcing retribution — she's consulting her conscience, very politely, very reasonably:
'I think he ought to have a little pepper? Just a few grains? I think the young man's tricks and manners make a claim upon his friends for a little pepper?'
Those question marks are everything — she's being scrupulously fair about it, conducting a little internal tribunal.
And the verdict is: yes, a little pepper seems proportionate.
Jenny Wren is the novel's great truth-teller, isn't she — but her truths come dressed as whimsy.
'A claim upon his friends' — that phrase works because it takes Fledgeby's own language of social obligation and turns it against him.
She's a child who has suffered enormously, and she uses laughter as armour.
The comedy isn't escapism — it's a way of bearing what cannot otherwise be borne.
That is well said, and I think it goes to the heart of why the comic passages in this novel feel earned rather than ornamental.
Jenny Wren's mischief is not mere high spirits.
It is a form of moral agency — perhaps the only form available to her.
From pepper to the dust heap — and perhaps the most purely physical comedy in the entire novel.
Silas Wegg being thrown into a scavenger's cart by Sloppy — I defy anyone to read this passage without laughing out loud.
The beauty is in the detail — 'his wooden leg in a highly unaccommodating state.'
That phrase — 'unaccommodating state' — applied to a wooden leg — the prose is barely containing its own delight.
And then this extraordinary sentence — let me read it properly:
'Sloppy lightly trotted out with him and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street door.'

'Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents.'
'A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash.'
A prodigious splash — that full stop is a masterpiece of comic timing.
What I notice is how formally the sentence is constructed — 'a somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity' — and then the bathos of that splash.
The legal precision of 'Mr S.' — as if this were a court report on proceedings of the utmost gravity.
And Wegg ends where he began — in the dust.
The comedy and the moral structure are the same gesture.
One observes that the novel is quite careful to give Sloppy the decisive physical act.
Sloppy is himself a figure of low comedy — the orphan boy who does impressions of newspapers — and yet here he is the instrument of justice.
The comedy, as Miss Woodcourt suggests, is not incidental — it is the argument.
And before we close this segment, Oliver — there is one more passage I want you to read.
The novel's emotional resolution — Mrs Boffin explaining why John Harmon kept postponing the revelation.
This passage — I confess it gets to me every time, and I've read it dozens of times.
It's comic and tender together — that mixture that is the novel's greatest achievement.
Mrs Boffin is explaining John Harmon's repeated deferrals — and the language he uses each time is the same:
'She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer.'
That repeated phrase — 'I must wait a little longer' — it's comic in its absurdity, a man deferring his own happiness because his wife is too good.
And then Mrs Boffin ends: 'and the horses is in, and the story is done, and God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all.'
'The horses is in' — the grammar is Mrs Boffin's, entirely her own — and the blessing is the whole novel's.
That moment is why the comedy matters so much throughout the novel.
It has trained us to feel warmth and irony at the same time — so that when the warmth arrives unguarded, it's almost unbearable.
Mrs Boffin in that moment is the novel's heart — and she gets there through 'the horses is in.'
I would only add that the comedy of this novel is inseparable from its generosity.
The novelist who can make Silas Wegg land in a dustcart with a prodigious splash is the same novelist who can make Mrs Boffin's blessing feel like grace.
That range is not common.
Not common at all.
From skeletons in closets to prodigious splashes to horses being in — this novel's comic voice is, as we've been hearing, a form of moral intelligence.
In our next segment, we turn to the novel's darker currents — the Thames, the dust heaps, and the question of what this world is built upon.

segments.title: The Boffin Transformation: Wealth, Corruption, and Redemption

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most richly comic and unsettling preoccupations: what sudden wealth does to a person, and to everyone around them.
The Boffins sit at the centre of that question — the Golden Dustman and his wife, inheritors of a fortune built from rubbish.
With me today are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the patience and moral seriousness of a lifetime spent with great fiction.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more of this novel aloud than almost any living person, and hears things in the prose the rest of us miss.
And Caroline Woodcourt brings the close attention of someone who has lived with these pages since she was a teenager.
Let's begin with the flood of letters that descends on Boffin the moment his fortune becomes public — a passage of extraordinary satirical energy.
The moment I encountered that chapter, I knew Dickens was writing it purely for performance.
The sheer accumulation — fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs — is comic architecture.
Each number is slightly wrong, slightly too precise, which is exactly where the joke lives.
And then Dickens delivers the ducal letter with a straight face that would make any actor weep with envy.
He sets it up with this glorious line — and I must read it, because it deserves to be heard:
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Every word is doing work there — 'large,' 'fat,' 'private,' 'double' — four adjectives of pompous self-importance before we even reach the coronet.
And then the postscript — 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas' — delivered as an afterthought of breathtaking condescension.
What strikes me is how precisely Dickens locates the moral failure here — and it is not Boffin's failure at all.
The Duke of Linseed is the figure of corruption in that passage — a nobleman lending his name, his coronet, his postscript, in exchange for nothing whatsoever of genuine charity.
Dickens tells us the letter was lithographed by the hundred — 'presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand.'
The aristocracy, in other words, has industrialised its condescension.
Burke would have found this as distressing as Dickens does — rank without responsibility is mere ornament.
What Dickens is anatomising here is not wealth per se, but the corruption of generosity into transaction.
But the individual beggars in the very next passage — they haunt me quite differently.
There's a moment where the comedy tips, just slightly, into something more uncomfortable.
Dickens gives us this devastating comparison about their letters and enclosures:
'they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That simile is so exactly right — and so strangely tender underneath the cruelty.
These people have taken whatever scraps of dignity they possess and tried to make them into something official.
And Dickens sees that — even while he's laughing at it.
That's precisely it — the categories are comic, but the desperation inside them is real.
The beggars of punctual business-habits — those who will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday if no postal order arrives — that is both hilarious and genuinely terrible.
The precision of 'a quarter to one P.M.' is the joke — but the suicide threat is underneath it, quite real.
When I read that passage aloud, I always feel the audience go slightly still at that point.
And this brings us, I think, to the novel's central moral proposition about wealth.
The Boffins are not destroyed by their inheritance — not ultimately.
Mr Boffin's apparent corruption — his miserliness, his cruelty to Rokesmith — turns out to be a performance, a staged education of Bella Wilfer.
Some readers find that a cheat. I do not.
I think Dickens is insisting that goodness of character can survive the assault of fortune — that Boffin is proof of that.
I want to bring Bella into this — because her arc is really inseparable from the Boffin question.
There's a moment early in her time at the Boffins' where she's furious at Rokesmith for even existing in her vicinity, and she thinks to herself:
'A little too much, I think, to have Pa's lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off!'
What's wonderful is how Dickens makes us see Bella's vanity and her charm simultaneously.
She is infuriating in that moment, and absolutely alive.
The corruption the Boffin wealth nearly works on her is perfectly legible — and her escape from it feels genuinely earned.
Her escape is sealed in a scene of domestic simplicity that I find rather beautiful — a shared supper in impoverished circumstances.
Dickens reaches for a fairy-tale register, which is exactly right.
He writes:

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
That 'even R. Wilfer' — the little comic aside about the father — is Dickens at his most affectionate.
He has earned the tenderness of that scene by showing us everything Bella had to relinquish to arrive at it.
And the detail of the brass knobs staring 'like the eyes of some dull dragon' — the office safe intruding on their domestic paradise.
The world of commerce and transaction can't be shut out entirely — it's still there, watching — but it has been reduced to something merely dull.
That's the redemption Dickens offers — not the removal of the dragon, but its domestication.
But the novel doesn't offer that consolation to everyone — and Bradley Headstone is where the darkness has no resolution at all.
The passage where he rehearses how he might have murdered Wrayburn better — it's almost unbearable to read.
He's not haunted by guilt in any redemptive sense.
He's haunted by the technical failure of the thing.
The prose enacts it with terrible precision.
Listen to the rhythm of the suppositions:
'Supposing his head had been held down under water for a while. Supposing the first blow had been truer. Supposing he had been shot. Supposing he had been strangled.'
'Suppose this way, that way, the other way. Suppose anything but getting unchained from the one idea, for that was inexorably impossible.'
The repetition of 'Suppose' is not rhetorical ornamentation — it is the sound of a mind that cannot stop.
Bradley Headstone is chained — that word appears twice — chained to a single idea, as a man might be chained to a corpse.
There's also that earlier line — 'To batter a man down from behind in the dark, on the brink of a river, was well enough' — delivered as though it were a minor tactical criticism.
The cold dispassion of 'was well enough' is what makes it so deeply wrong — Dickens is inside a murderer's reasoning.
This is not satire. This is something darker — a portrait of a consciousness that has entirely foreclosed on conscience.
And so the novel holds all of this simultaneously — the comedy of the Duke's lithographed charity appeal, Bella's vanity and transformation, the fairy-tale supper, and Bradley's unrelenting darkness.
What Dickens seems to insist upon is that wealth is a test — not the only test, but a sharp one — and that character is revealed, not created, by money.
After the break, we'll be turning to the river — the Thames as presence, as judge, as grave — and to what the novel makes of water in all its forms.

segments.title: Dickens in the Details: Atmosphere and Technique in the Novel's Darker Moments

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
In this segment we're turning our attention to something Dickens does almost invisibly — the way atmosphere is built, sentence by sentence, detail by detail.
A room can encode an entire social argument. A staircase can become a gothic nightmare. A couple walking away down a street can carry the weight of moral judgment.
With us for this close reading is Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has performed more classic novels than anyone should probably admit to.
Oliver, you hear this novel the way the rest of us only read it. Let's start with the Bower.
The Bower is one of Dickens's great comic interiors, and I mean that in the fullest sense — it is architecture as comedy.
Before a single character speaks, the room itself performs.
Dickens announces it with complete confidence — the sentence is a drumroll.
"It was the queerest of rooms, fitted and furnished more like a luxurious amateur tap-room than anything else within the ken of Silas Wegg."
"Luxurious amateur tap-room" — three words that contain an entire social predicament.
The Boffins have money but no map for how to spend it, and the room tells you that before Mrs Boffin opens her mouth.
And then Dickens catalogues the room with this marvellous observational eye — he never rushes it.
The eight volumes are laid flat in a row, and he says they look — here, let me find it —
"like a galvanic battery."
A galvanic battery! He could have said "in a row" and stopped there. But no — it has to crackle with energy.
And then comes my favourite detail — the carpet's glowing vegetation simply stops short at Mrs Boffin's footstool, and gives way to sand and sawdust.
You have two worlds sharing one room, one floor — and the border runs right through the middle of it.
That border is doing real work, isn't it — the novel keeps drawing these lines between the respectable and the vital.
But there are passages in this novel where the atmosphere turns something much darker. The gothic Dickens.
Oliver, the scene outside Wrayburn's chambers — Bradley Headstone on the staircase. That's a passage written for performance.
It is — and it's written for a very particular kind of performance. Almost no sound. Almost no movement.
Look at how Dickens describes Bradley ascending that staircase. He doesn't say "Headstone crept up the stairs."
He says: "The haggard head floated up the dark staircase."
Just the head. Disembodied. Floating. The body has been dissolved by obsession — only the watching, listening, suffering head remains.
And then the narrator delivers his coup de grâce with perfect coolness.

"If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night."
That "might have been less disposed to sleep" — the narrator is practically winking. It's the understatement of a man describing a horror.
The novel's darkest passages sometimes arrive inside a single, very quiet sentence.
There's a moment in John Harmon's confession — if we can call it that — when he reads his own death notice posted at Whitehall.
Oliver, that passage carries a weight that's almost vertiginous.
Vertiginous is exactly the word. When I recorded it, I had to stop.
A man reads a placard announcing his own death, goes to view his own corpse, and understands — in that same appalling moment — the full structure of the conspiracy against him.
Dickens holds all of that in one long, breathless sentence. Listen to how it lands.

"I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide, when the stream ran deep and strong."
"The same dark place into the same dark tide" — the repetition does something almost musical. It insists on the symmetry of two fates.
Murder and near-murder, bound together by money, by the river, by the dark.
The river runs through this novel as both literal place and moral condition. And there's one more passage I want to consider — the departure of the Lammles.
It's not gothic, not comic in any warm sense — it's something else entirely. Oliver?
It's a farewell written with a kind of terrible elegance. Dickens refuses to give them a dramatic exit — they simply walk away.
Arm-in-arm, showily enough — but without exchanging a syllable. The performance of a marriage, with nothing underneath.
Dickens offers one simile — they have, he suggests, something of the shamed air of two cheats linked by concealed handcuffs — and then he sets it aside.
Because the real sentence, the sentence that counts, is the one that ends it all.
"In turning the street corner they might have turned out of this world, for anything Mr and Mrs Boffin ever saw of them to the contrary."
"Turned out of this world." That is the whole moral verdict, delivered as a geographical observation.
They vanish around a corner and the novel simply — closes the door on them. No funeral, no catastrophe. Just erasure.
Erasure. That is perhaps the most chilling sentence of punishment Dickens ever wrote — not a curse, just an absence.

We've moved today from the comic geography of the Bower to the gothic dread on Wrayburn's staircase, through the vertiginous horror of John Harmon's discovery, and out into that cold street with the Lammles.
What connects them is Dickens's absolute command of atmosphere as moral instrument.
In our next segment, we turn to the characters themselves — the comic grotesques, the suffering heroes, and those who are somewhere in between.

segments.title: Closing: Our Mutual Friend and the Stakes of Connection

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through a novel that is, at its heart, about what connects us — and what corrodes those connections.
Before we close, I want to bring us back to character — specifically to two women whose inner lives Dickens renders with extraordinary precision.
Bella Wilfer and Lizzie Hexam — one caught in the gravity of money, one caught in the gravity of love.
Caroline, you've been the novel's conscience in this room today — shall we begin with you?
What strikes me most about Bella is that Dickens gives her the remarkable gift of self-knowledge — and then shows us how useless self-knowledge can be.
She knows exactly what she is doing, she knows it is wrong, and she does it anyway.
There's this scene where she's alone in her room after Mr Boffin has offered her perfectly sound advice about money and ambition.
And she puts the question to herself — in the looking-glass, as usual — in language that is at once comic and genuinely damning.
'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then?'
'No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
That word — Beast — directed at herself, in the mirror.
There's something almost unbearable about that clarity — she sees herself and still cannot stop.
And the mirror — that looking-glass — does a great deal of work in this novel.
Bella's conscience operates through that reflection. She doesn't confide in a friend — she prosecutes herself.
And then — brilliantly — Dickens gives her the same scene with Lizzie Hexam present, but this time the punishment is physical.
Lizzie speaks of selfless love, and Bella's conscience convicts her on the spot.
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
And she gives herself — I love this — a penitential poke in the side.
Dickens is very funny, and the funniness here is entirely in service of something real about moral awakening.
Oliver is right to press on that comic mode — and I think it's worth saying why it matters morally, not merely theatrically.
Bella is not satirised from without — she is satirised from within herself.
That is the difference between a caricature and a character.
And against Bella's mercenary confusion, Dickens sets Lizzie — whose feelings are entirely without calculation.
What Lizzie says about Eugene Wrayburn — a man who has brought her nothing but danger and grief — is one of the most quietly devastating lines in the book.
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
That is not sentiment. That is the grammar of genuine love — measured, clear-eyed, and completely without self-pity.
And what Dickens gives us in that moment is the intimacy of confession — Lizzie has never spoken any of this aloud before.
She says, 'I had no thought of ever parting with a single word of it, a moment before you came in; but you came in, and my mind changed.'
The novel argues, quietly, that connection itself is what opens us.
Bella is transformed not by instruction but by proximity to Lizzie's honesty.
That's the secret architecture of the whole book, I think.
Everyone in it is being watched — by each other, by us — and the question is whether being seen will save you or destroy you.
Bella looks in the mirror and calls herself a Beast. Lizzie looks at Bella and opens like a door.
And the novel survives, I would argue, precisely because it does not resolve that tension cheaply.
Money corrodes, love endures — but only at cost.
Dickens earns the resolutions he allows. He earns them through exactly the kind of self-examination we've been discussing.
I think that's a remarkable note to end on — the idea that the novel earns what it gives.
My thanks to Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who have made this novel's world feel very present today.
Our Mutual Friend is a great, dark, comic, humane novel — and if you haven't read it, or haven't read it recently, I hope today has sent you back to it.
Thank you for listening.

c25:p0.text:
The minion of fortune and the worm of the hour, or in less cutting
      language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, the Golden Dustman, had become as
      much at home in his eminently aristocratic family mansion as he was likely
      ever to be. He could not but feel that, like an eminently aristocratic
      family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite
      amount of parasites; but he was content to regard this drawback on his
      property as a sort of perpetual Legacy Duty. He felt the more resigned to
      it, forasmuch as Mrs Boffin enjoyed herself completely, and Miss Bella was
      delighted.
c25:p0.summary: Nicodemus Boffin, the newly wealthy Golden Dustman, has settled into his grand mansion, finding it oversized but content because Mrs Boffin and Bella are delighted.
c25:p0.best_quote: like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites

c40:p97.text:
For, Silas Wegg felt it to be quite out of the question that he could lay
      his head upon his pillow in peace, without first hovering over Mr Boffin’s
      house in the superior character of its Evil Genius. Power (unless it be
      the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the
      lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with
      his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a
      house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.
c40:p97.summary: Wegg cannot rest without hovering over Boffin's house, fantasizing about his power to destroy it, demonstrating how power appeals to base natures.
c40:p97.best_quote: Power (unless it be the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.

c40:p31.text:
‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and
      residue of his property to the Crown.’
c40:p31.summary: Wegg describes the will's contents: John Harmon leaves the Little Mound to Boffin and the remainder to the Crown, having no close relationships.
c40:p31.best_quote: Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c38:p42.text:
Bella ventured for a moment to look stealthily towards him under her
      eyelashes, and she saw a dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and
      conceit, overshadowing the once open face.
c38:p42.summary: Bella observes a dark expression of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit shadowing Mr Boffin's formerly open countenance.
c38:p42.best_quote: A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.

c38:p47.text:
‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an
      unctuous manner. ‘R—r—rich!’
c38:p47.summary: Mr Boffin emphatically advises Bella to pursue money above all else, declaring that she should capitalize on her beauty and the wealth they will bestow on her to become and remain rich.
c38:p47.best_quote: Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.
c31:p109.best_quote: Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!

c31:p125.text:
The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled,
      and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the
      determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the
      streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.
c31:p125.summary: Rokesmith watches from a doorway as Betty departs with steady determination, then observes Bella standing alone—a moment that captures his emotional detachment and the poignancy of their separation.
c31:p125.best_quote: The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’
c8:p39.summary: Boffin details how he and Mrs Boffin repeatedly defended young John Harmon against Old Harmon's cruelty, including an incident where Harmon struck Mrs Boffin and she collapsed, establishing their selfless advocacy for the boy.
c8:p39.best_quote: I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard... and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.

c9:p23.text:
Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our
      fire? Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it’s come to us, I
      should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and
      give him John’s name, and provide for him. Somehow, it would make me
      easier, I fancy. Say it’s only a whim—’
c9:p23.summary: Mrs Boffin proposes adopting an orphan child, naming him John Harmon in memory of the young heir who drowned, thereby using their inherited fortune for redemptive good.
c9:p23.best_quote: Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.

c64:p97.text:
‘That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills
      made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything
      absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and
      reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.
      That Dutch bottle was found by my noble benefactor and yours, after he
      entered on possession of the estate. That Dutch bottle distressed him
      beyond measure, because, though I and my sister were both no more, it cast
      a slur upon our memory which he knew we had done nothing in our miserable
      youth, to deserve. That Dutch bottle, therefore, he buried in the Mound
      belonging to him, and there it lay while you, you thankless wretch, were
      prodding and poking—often very near it, I dare say. His intention
      was, that it should never see the light; but he was afraid to destroy it,
      lest to destroy such a document, even with his great generous motive,
      might be an offence at law. After the discovery was made here who I was,
      Mr Boffin, still restless on the subject, told me, upon certain conditions
      impossible for such a hound as you to appreciate, the secret of that Dutch
      bottle. I urged upon him the necessity of its being dug up, and the paper
      being legally produced and established. The first thing you saw him do,
      and the second thing has been done without your knowledge. Consequently,
      the paper now rattling in your hand as I shake you—and I should like
      to shake the life out of you—is worth less than the rotten cork of
      the Dutch bottle, do you understand?’
c64:p97.summary: Harmon explains how the Dutch bottle was found by Boffin after entering the estate, buried in the Mound to hide its contents, and later exhumed without Wegg's knowledge.
c64:p97.best_quote: That Dutch bottle, scoundrel, contained the latest will of the many wills made by my unhappy self-tormenting father. That will gives everything absolutely to my noble benefactor and yours, Mr Boffin, excluding and reviling me, and my sister (then already dead of a broken heart), by name.

c64:p99.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ said John Harmon, taking another sailor-like turn on his
      cravat and holding him in his corner at arms’ length, ‘I shall make two
      more short speeches to you, because I hope they will torment you. Your
      discovery was a genuine discovery (such as it was), for nobody had thought
      of looking into that place. Neither did we know you had made it, until
      Venus spoke to Mr Boffin, though I kept you under good observation from my
      first appearance here, and though Sloppy has long made it the chief
      occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow. I tell
      you this, that you may know we knew enough of you to persuade Mr Boffin to
      let us lead you on, deluded, to the last possible moment, in order that
      your disappointment might be the heaviest possible disappointment. That’s
      the first short speech, do you understand?’
c64:p99.summary: Harmon explains that they discovered Wegg's find through Venus, watched him closely, and deliberately prolonged his deception to maximize his disappointment.

How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now,

c22:p66.text:
‘And this fellow,’ exclaimed Lammle, stopping and making the most of his
      chest—‘This fellow presumes on my having selected him out of all the
      young fellows I know, for an advantageous opportunity! This fellow
      presumes on my having in my desk round the corner, his dirty note of hand
      for a wretched sum payable on the occurrence of a certain event, which
      event can only be of my and my wife’s bringing about! This fellow,
      Fledgeby, presumes to be impertinent to me, Lammle. Give me your nose

‘I think,’ said Miss Jenny with a silent laugh, ‘he ought to have a little

The words were but out of his mouth when John Harmon lifted his finger,

      buttons almost as prominently on view as Sloppy’s own, and with his wooden
      leg in a highly unaccommodating state. But, not for many seconds was his
      countenance visible in the room; for, Sloppy lightly trotted out with him
      and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street
      door. Mr Sloppy’s instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road;
      but, a scavenger’s cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with
      its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to
      resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart’s contents.
      A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a

c63:p42.text:
‘And so, my good and pretty,’ pursued Mrs Boffin, ‘you was married, and
      there was we hid up in the church-organ by this husband of yours; for he
      wouldn’t let us out with it then, as was first meant. “No,” he says,
      “she’s so unselfish and contented, that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I
      must wait a little longer.” Then, when baby was expected, he says, “She is
      such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I
      must wait a little longer.” Then when baby was born, he says, “She is so
      much better than she ever was, that I can’t afford to be rich yet. I must
      wait a little longer.” And so he goes on and on, till I says outright,
      “Now, John, if you don’t fix a time for setting her up in her own house
      and home, and letting us walk out of it, I’ll turn Informer.” Then he says
      he’ll only wait to triumph beyond what we ever thought possible, and to
      show her to us better than even we ever supposed; and he says, “She shall
      see me under suspicion of having murdered myself, and  you  shall see how
      trusting and how true she’ll be.” Well! Noddy and me agreed to that, and
      he was right, and here you are, and the horses is in, and the story is
      done, and God bless you my Beauty, and God bless us all!’
c63:p42.summary: Mrs Boffin completes the narrative: John repeatedly postponed revealing himself because Bella kept improving; only after much urging does he agree to test her by allowing her to witness suspicion of his involvement in his own murder.
c63:p42.best_quote: She is such a cheerful, glorious housewife that I can't afford to be rich yet. I must wait a little longer.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c25:p17.text:
‘A little too much, I think,’ Miss Bella reflected scornfully, ‘to have
      Pa’s lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off! A little
      too much, indeed, to have the opportunities opened to me by Mr and Mrs
      Boffin, appropriated by a mere Secretary and Pa’s lodger!’
c25:p17.summary: Bella internally rails against Rokesmith's presumption in claiming her attention and excluding eligible suitors.
c25:p17.best_quote: to have Pa's lodger laying claim to me, and keeping eligible people off!

c49:p79.text:
It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three
      nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous
      low growlings of the alarming discovery, ‘Somebody’s been drinking  my 
      milk!’ It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or
      John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made. The uncongenial oddity of
      its surroundings, with the two brass knobs of the iron safe of Chicksey,
      Veneering, and Stobbles staring from a corner, like the eyes of some dull
      dragon, only made it the more delightful.
c49:p79.summary: The narrator poetically describes their simple meal as surpassing all previous experience—like the fairy tale feast of the three hobgoblins, but without threat or discord.
